messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi's eyes still widened at the slightest creak of the old wooden floorboards in his house. It was a sound that transported him back to that fateful night when he was assaulted by a group of strangers while working late on a plumbing job. The memories of that event were seared into his mind like vivid, disturbing images – the glint of metal, the feeling of being pinned down, and the sound of footsteps echoing through the abandoned building. Those pictures haunted him every time he tried to fall asleep, making it impossible for him to shut off his brain. Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a plumber, but since that night, he couldn't shake the feeling that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. The thought of walking into a dark, abandoned building or working late hours made his heart racing with anxiety. He started to doubt whether he could trust himself to do the right thing in critical situations. His wife noticed the change in him and tried to reassure him, but Kofi couldn't help feeling like he'd lost his edge. This sense of inadequacy made him feel like he was walking on eggshells all the time, waiting for something to go wrong. As a result, Kofi became increasingly withdrawn, only feeling safe within the confines of his own home. He stopped taking on new projects and started turning down jobs that required working in isolated areas or late hours. His business began to suffer, but he couldn't bring himself to venture out into the world again. The injustice of what had happened to him still burned deep within him – nothing had been done about it, no one was held accountable, and Kofi felt like he'd been left to pick up the pieces on his own. One day, while working in his garage, Kofi's wife asked him to take a look at a leaky faucet. As he approached the sink, he noticed a faint movement out of the corner of his eye – it was just their cat, but for a split second, Kofi's heart skipped a beat. He froze, his mind racing back to that night, and suddenly those vivid memories came flooding back. The images were so intense that they left him gasping for air, feeling like he'd been punched in the gut. Kofi tried to brush it off as mere paranoia, but deep down, he knew he was struggling to cope with the aftermath of the assault. He started to question whether he would ever be able to reclaim his sense of self-worth and confidence. His wife encouraged him to seek help, but Kofi was hesitant – what if talking about it made things worse? What if he couldn't trust himself to confront those memories head-on? As the days turned into weeks, Kofi realized that he needed professional help. He couldn't keep living in this state of perpetual fear and self-doubt. With a mix of trepidation and hope, he scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping that she could guide him through the darkness and back to a place where he felt safe – not just in his own home but within himself. When Kofi finally sat down with the therapist, he broke down in tears, overcome by the guilt and shame of what had happened. The images still haunted him, but for the first time in months, he began to feel like there was a way out – that maybe, just maybe, he could learn to put those memories into words and start rebuilding his shattered sense of self.
